subject: History of USA
title: 10. Role of the USA in the United Nations and International Organizations (1945–2012)

segments.text: After 1945 the U.S. chose to build permanent international institutions rather than repeat the limited post-1919 approach (Topic 8) — but real tension persists between multilateral rules and U.S. willingness to act independently, and a strong answer distinguishes institutions the U.S. helped create from cases where it acted outside or alongside them.

U.S. policy has included Security Council diplomacy, sanctions, peacekeeping support and military action under varying legal arrangements — the Korean War and Gulf War are major examples of genuinely multilateral security action. At the same time, U.S. governments have sometimes acted without broad international support (the 2003 Iraq War is the key case), generating controversy over sovereignty and international law. The United States is powerful but cannot simply “control” international organisations; rules, other member states, vetoes, voting blocs and domestic politics all constrain outcomes.

items.text: The IMF and World Bank, created during WWII to promote monetary stability and reconstruction, with strong ongoing U.S. influence.

Organise institutions by function: collective security, economic/financial, trade, and military alliances; for each, note why the U.S. supported it, what power it exercises, and where tension with multilateral rules arose.
Do not write that the United States owns or controls the UN.
Do not confuse the UN with NATO or the IMF; they have different purposes and decision systems.
Do not judge U.S. multilateralism only by membership; compare support for institutions with cases of unilateral action.
The U.S. is a permanent UN Security Council member with veto power.
The IMF and World Bank emerged from Bretton Woods with strong U.S. influence; GATT (1948) evolved into the WTO (1995).
The U.S. was a founding NATO member (1949).
Distinguish institutions the U.S. helped build (UN, Bretton Woods, GATT/WTO, NATO) from cases of unilateral action (2003 Iraq) — both belong in a balanced answer.
U.S. influence within international organisations is real but bounded by rules, other states, and domestic politics — never “control.”
